def: A finite, step-by-step procedure that solves a problem.
see: Complexity Analysis and Amortized Analysis

def: The average cost per operation over a worst-case sequence of operations, even if single operations are sometimes expensive (a dynamic array append is O(1) amortized).
see: Complexity Analysis and Amortized Analysis

def: A block of equal-sized elements stored one after another in memory, reached by index.
see: Dynamic Arrays

def: A self-balancing binary search tree whose subtree heights never differ by more than 1.
see: Self-Balancing Trees: AVL, Red-Black, Treaps and Skip Lists

def: A wide, balanced search tree whose nodes hold many keys, designed so each node fills one disk page or cache block.
see: B-Trees, B+ Trees and LSM Trees

def: Search that builds a solution step by step and undoes a step when it leads nowhere.
see: Backtracking, Branch and Bound, and Bitmask DP

def: A way to describe how running time or memory grows with input size, ignoring constant factors; O(n) means roughly proportional to n.
see: Complexity Analysis and Amortized Analysis

def: Finding a value in a sorted array by repeatedly halving the range; O(log n).
see: Binary Search and Its Variants

def: A compact structure that answers 'possibly in the set' or 'definitely not'; it never gives false negatives.
see: Probabilistic Structures: Bloom, Count-Min, HyperLogLog and Consistent Hashing

def: Graph traversal that visits vertices in layers of increasing distance from the start, using a queue.
see: Graph Representations and Traversals

def: A small fast store of recent or popular results; a replacement policy (LRU, LFU, CLOCK) decides what to evict when full.
see: Caches: LRU, LFU, CLOCK and Belady's OPT

def: The unit (typically 64 bytes) in which memory moves between RAM and the CPU cache; why contiguous data is fast.
see: Performance-Oriented C: Caches, Branches, Data Layout and Vectorization

def: An atomic CPU instruction that writes a new value only if the location still holds an expected value; the building block of lock-free code.
see: Concurrent and Lock-Free Structures

def: How the running time or memory use of an algorithm grows with input size.
see: Complexity Analysis and Amortized Analysis

def: Graph traversal that follows a path as deep as possible before backing up, using a stack or recursion.
see: Graph Representations and Traversals

def: Shortest paths from one vertex in a graph with non-negative edge weights.
see: Shortest Paths: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall and A*

def: Solving a problem by combining answers to overlapping subproblems, each computed once.
see: Dynamic Programming

def: The minimum number of single-character insertions, deletions and substitutions turning one string into another (Levenshtein distance).
see: String Matching and Edit Distance

def: A set of vertices (nodes) connected by edges; models networks, dependencies, maps.
see: Graph Representations and Traversals

def: Builds a solution by always taking the locally best choice; correct only for problems where that is provably safe.
see: Greedy Algorithms

def: A function that turns a key into a fixed-size number, ideally spreading keys evenly.
see: Hash Tables: Open Addressing, Deletion, Cuckoo and Hash Flooding

def: A structure mapping keys to values in expected O(1) time by using a hash of the key as an array index.
see: Hash Tables: Open Addressing, Deletion, Cuckoo and Hash Flooding

def: A tree stored in an array where each parent is no larger than its children, giving fast access to the minimum.
see: Heaps and Priority Queues

def: The region of memory used for dynamic allocation (malloc/free). Not the same as the heap data structure.
see: Dynamic Memory: malloc Internals, Classic Bugs and Custom Allocators

def: A condition that holds before and after every step of a loop or operation; used to prove code correct.
see: Recursion, Divide and Conquer, and Loop Invariants

def: A chain of nodes each pointing to the next; cheap insertion, slow indexing.
see: Linked Lists

def: A concurrency guarantee that some thread always makes progress even if others are paused.
see: Concurrent and Lock-Free Structures

def: A cache policy that evicts the entry unused for the longest time.
see: Caches: LRU, LFU, CLOCK and Belady's OPT

def: A write-optimised store that buffers writes in memory and merges sorted files in the background (LevelDB, RocksDB, Cassandra).
see: B-Trees, B+ Trees and LSM Trees

def: Caching the result of a function call so repeated calls with the same input are free.
see: Dynamic Programming

def: The cheapest set of edges that connects all vertices of a graph.
see: Union-Find, Spanning Trees, Connectivity and Max-Flow

def: A first-in, first-out collection.
see: Stacks, Queues, Deques and Ring Buffers

def: A function that solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller instance.
see: Recursion, Divide and Conquer, and Loop Invariants

def: A self-balancing binary search tree using node colours; the basis of many library maps.
see: Self-Balancing Trees: AVL, Red-Black, Treaps and Skip Lists

def: A fixed-size queue stored in an array that wraps around.
see: Stacks, Queues, Deques and Ring Buffers

def: A last-in, first-out collection.
see: Stacks, Queues, Deques and Ring Buffers

def: An ordering of a directed acyclic graph's vertices so every edge goes forward; used for dependency resolution.
see: Graph Representations and Traversals

def: A tree indexed by the characters or bits of a key, used for prefix lookups and IP routing.
see: Tries, Radix Trees and Longest-Prefix Match

def: A structure that tracks which elements belong to the same group, with near-constant-time merge and lookup.
see: Union-Find, Spanning Trees, Connectivity and Max-Flow

def: The binary-level contract between compiled code: calling convention, type sizes and layout, symbol naming.
see: Stack Frames and the x86-64 System V Calling Convention

def: A number identifying a location in memory.
see: Pointers, Arrays and Decay

def: The rule that data of a given size must sit at an address that is a multiple of some number (often its size).
see: Structs, Alignment, Padding, Unions, Bit-fields and Endianness

def: Writing past the end of an array or buffer, corrupting neighbouring memory; a leading source of security bugs.
see: Strings and Buffer Safety

def: A program that translates source code into machine code (or an intermediate form).
see: The Compilation Pipeline and the ELF Object Model

def: A pointer to memory that has been freed or has gone out of scope.
see: Dynamic Memory: malloc Internals, Classic Bugs and Custom Allocators

def: Executable and Linkable Format: the standard file format for programs, object files and shared libraries on Linux.
see: The Compilation Pipeline and the ELF Object Model

def: The order in which the bytes of a multi-byte number are stored (little-endian: least significant byte first).
see: Structs, Alignment, Padding, Unions, Bit-fields and Endianness

def: A .h file declaring functions and types so other source files can use them.
see: The Preprocessor and Macros

def: The tool that combines object files and libraries into one executable or shared library, resolving symbols.
see: Static and Shared Libraries, Symbols, Dynamic Loading

def: A text substitution performed by the preprocessor before compilation.
see: The Preprocessor and Macros

def: Allocated memory that is never freed and can no longer be reached.
see: Dynamic Memory: malloc Internals, Classic Bugs and Custom Allocators

def: A pointer that refers to nothing; dereferencing it is undefined behavior.
see: Pointers, Arrays and Decay

def: The compiler's output for one source file: machine code plus symbols, not yet runnable.
see: The Compilation Pipeline and the ELF Object Model

def: A variable that holds the address of another object.
see: Pointers for Beginners

def: The first compilation stage; expands #include and #define before the compiler proper runs.
see: The Preprocessor and Macros

def: A compiler-inserted runtime checker (AddressSanitizer, UBSan, ThreadSanitizer) that detects memory and concurrency bugs.
see: Debugging with gdb and the Sanitizers

def: The crash the operating system delivers when a program touches memory it may not access.
see: Debugging with gdb and the Sanitizers

def: The memory region holding each function call's local variables and return address.
see: Stack Frames and the x86-64 System V Calling Convention

def: Code bundled with a program at link time (.a) versus loaded when the program runs (.so).
see: Static and Shared Libraries, Symbols, Dynamic Loading

def: A named function or variable in an object file, resolved by the linker.
see: Static and Shared Libraries, Symbols, Dynamic Loading

def: Code the C standard places no requirements on; the compiler may assume it never happens, so results can be anything.
see: C Standards, the Abstract Machine and Undefined Behavior

def: Accessing memory after it has been freed; undefined behavior and a common exploit.
see: Dynamic Memory: malloc Internals, Classic Bugs and Custom Allocators

def: A C qualifier telling the compiler a variable may change outside the program's control, so every access must really happen.
see: Qualifiers, Storage Classes, Scope and Linkage

def: One slice of root's power (for example binding low ports) that can be granted to a process separately.
see: Users, Permissions, ACLs and Capabilities

def: A kernel feature that limits and accounts for CPU, memory and I/O used by a group of processes.
see: systemd Timers, cgroups v2 and Resource Control

def: An ordinary process (group) isolated with namespaces and limited with cgroups; not a virtual machine.
see: Linux Namespaces — The Isolation Primitive Behind Containers

def: A background process, usually started at boot, that provides a service.
see: systemd — Units, Dependencies, Targets, Hardening and the Journal

def: Kernel code that lets the operating system talk to a particular piece of hardware.
see: Kernel Modules, Device Drivers and udev

def: A way to run small, verified programs inside the kernel for tracing, networking and security.
see: eBPF — Programmable Kernel Observability, Networking and Security

def: A Linux system call for efficiently waiting on many file descriptors at once.
see: Event-Driven I/O: select, poll, epoll and io_uring

def: A small integer a process uses to refer to an open file, socket or pipe.
see: Filesystem Hierarchy, VFS, Inodes, Links and File Descriptors

def: The structure on a disk that organises data into files and directories (ext4, XFS, Btrfs).
see: ext4, XFS, Btrfs, Journaling and Durability (fsync)

def: fork duplicates the current process; exec replaces a process's program with a new one. Together they start every program.
see: Process Lifecycle — fork, exec, wait

def: The first process the kernel starts; on most systems it is systemd and it adopts orphaned processes.
see: The Boot Process — Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, initramfs and init

def: A small temporary root filesystem the kernel uses during boot to find and mount the real root.
see: The Boot Process — Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, initramfs and init

def: The on-disk record describing a file (owner, permissions, size, data location); the file's name lives in a directory entry.
see: Filesystem Hierarchy, VFS, Inodes, Links and File Descriptors

def: systemd's structured log store; or a filesystem's write-ahead log that keeps the disk consistent after a crash.
see: systemd — Units, Dependencies, Targets, Hardening and the Journal

def: The core of the operating system: manages memory, processes, devices and system calls.
see: The Boot Process — Firmware, Bootloader, Kernel, initramfs and init

def: Code that can be loaded into the running kernel (often a driver).
see: Kernel Modules, Device Drivers and udev

def: Attaching a filesystem to a directory so its files appear in the directory tree.
see: Filesystem Hierarchy, VFS, Inodes, Links and File Descriptors

def: A kernel feature giving a process its own private view of a resource (PIDs, network, mounts...).
see: Linux Namespaces — The Isolation Primitive Behind Containers

def: The kernel mechanism that terminates a process when the system runs out of memory.
see: mmap, Overcommit, the OOM Killer, Huge Pages, NUMA and Swap

def: A tool (apt, dnf) that installs, upgrades and removes software and its dependencies.
see: Installing Software and Managing Services

def: RAM the kernel uses to keep recently read file data, making repeated reads fast.
see: Virtual Memory, Paging and the Page Cache

def: A one-way channel connecting one process's output to another's input (the | in the shell).
see: The Shell — Parsing, Expansion, Redirection, Pipes and Job Control

def: A running instance of a program with its own memory and resources.
see: Process Lifecycle — fork, exec, wait

def: Virtual filesystems exposing kernel and process information as files.
see: System Calls, the vDSO, strace, /proc, /sys and Netlink

def: The all-powerful administrative account (user ID 0).
see: Users, Permissions, ACLs and Capabilities

def: The kernel component that decides which process runs on which CPU and for how long.
see: The Linux Scheduler: Classes, EEVDF/CFS, Priorities, Affinity and CPU Limits

def: The program (bash, zsh) that reads your commands and runs them.
see: Linux Command Line Basics

def: A small asynchronous notification sent to a process (SIGINT from Ctrl-C, SIGTERM, SIGKILL).
see: Signals in Depth

def: Disk space used as overflow when RAM is full.
see: mmap, Overcommit, the OOM Killer, Huge Pages, NUMA and Swap

def: A request from a program to the kernel (read, write, open...).
see: System Calls, the vDSO, strace, /proc, /sys and Netlink

def: The init system and service manager on most distributions; starts services, tracks dependencies and logs.
see: systemd — Units, Dependencies, Targets, Hardening and the Journal

def: A path of execution inside a process; threads of one process share its memory.
see: Threads and Synchronization

def: Giving each process its own address space, mapped to physical RAM by the kernel and CPU.
see: Virtual Memory, Paging and the Page Cache

def: The kernel layer that gives all filesystems the same open/read/write interface.
see: Filesystem Hierarchy, VFS, Inodes, Links and File Descriptors

def: An ordered list of permit/deny rules used to filter traffic.
see: ACLs, Stateless vs Stateful Filtering and Infrastructure Protection

def: Address Resolution Protocol: finds the MAC address that goes with an IPv4 address on the local network.
see: ARP and IPv4 Address Conflict Detection

def: A network under one administrative control with its own routing policy, identified by an AS number; the unit BGP connects.
see: BGP-4 Fundamentals: Sessions, Messages, Attributes and Best-Path Selection

def: How much data a link can carry per second (not how fast one bit travels).
see: What Is a Network?

def: Border Gateway Protocol: the routing protocol that connects the Internet's autonomous systems.
see: BGP-4 Fundamentals: Sessions, Messages, Attributes and Best-Path Selection

def: A device that forwards Ethernet frames between ports by learning which MAC addresses are on which port.
see: Ethernet Frames and MAC Learning

def: Traffic delivered to every device on a local network segment.
see: Ethernet Frames and MAC Learning

def: Classless Inter-Domain Routing: writing a network as address/prefix-length, such as 10.1.0.0/16.
see: IPv4 Addressing, Subnetting, VLSM and CIDR

def: The set of devices that can interfere with each other's transmissions / that receive each other's broadcasts.
see: Ethernet Frames and MAC Learning

def: The router a host sends traffic to when the destination is not on its own network.
see: A Packet's Journey: Host to Gateway to Host

def: Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol: automatically gives a device an IP address and settings.
see: DHCP — Messages, Leases, Relay and Options

def: The Domain Name System: translates names like example.com into IP addresses.
see: What Is a Network?

def: Equal-cost multipath: sharing traffic over several routes of equal cost.
see: Forwarding: Routing Table, Longest-Prefix Match, Policy Routing and ECMP

def: Wrapping data in the header of each protocol layer as it goes down the stack.
see: Network Models, Encapsulation and Device Roles

def: The dominant wired local-network technology (IEEE 802.3); defines frames and MAC addresses.
see: Ethernet Frames and MAC Learning

def: Forwarding Information Base: the table the data plane actually uses to forward. Routing Information Base: all routes learned by routing protocols.
see: Forwarding: Routing Table, Longest-Prefix Match, Policy Routing and ECMP

def: Splitting an IP packet into smaller pieces to fit a link's MTU.
see: IPv4 Header, Fragmentation and MTU

def: The unit of data at Layer 2 (an Ethernet frame).
see: Ethernet Frames and MAC Learning

def: A router connecting a network to another network.
see: A Packet's Journey: Host to Gateway to Host

def: Interior gateway protocols (OSPF, IS-IS) route inside one organisation; exterior ones (BGP) between organisations.
see: Routing Fundamentals: Static Routes, Protocol Families and Convergence

def: A number identifying a network interface at Layer 3 (32-bit for IPv4, 128-bit for IPv6).
see: IPv4 Addressing, Subnetting, VLSM and CIDR

def: The successor to IPv4 with 128-bit addresses.
see: IPv6 Header, Extension Headers and Addressing

def: Link Aggregation Control Protocol: bundles several physical links into one logical link.
see: Link Aggregation (802.1AX / LACP) and Load Balancing

def: The time a bit takes to get from sender to receiver.
see: What Is a Network?

def: The data-link layer (frames, MAC addresses, switches) and the network layer (packets, IP addresses, routers).
see: Network Models, Encapsulation and Device Roles

def: Link-state database: every router's copy of the topology that link-state protocols use to compute routes.
see: OSPFv2 Operation: Neighbors, DR/BDR, Flooding and SPF

def: A 48-bit hardware address identifying a network interface on a local network.
see: Ethernet Frames and MAC Learning

def: The number a routing protocol uses to compare routes; lower is better.
see: Routing Fundamentals: Static Routes, Protocol Families and Convergence

def: A technique that forwards packets using short labels instead of IP lookups, used by providers for VPNs.
see: MPLS, LDP and MPLS L3VPN

def: Maximum transmission unit: the largest packet a link can carry (1500 bytes on standard Ethernet).
see: IPv4 Header, Fragmentation and MTU

def: Traffic sent once and delivered to a group of interested receivers.
see: IP Multicast Basics — Addressing, IGMP, MLD and Snooping

def: Network address translation: rewriting addresses (and ports) so many private hosts share a few public addresses.
see: NAT — Static, NAPT, Port Forwarding, Hairpinning and CGNAT

def: IPv6's replacement for ARP, plus router discovery and address autoconfiguration.
see: ICMPv6, Neighbor Discovery, SLAAC and DAD

def: A seven-layer reference model for network functions; real networks follow the simpler TCP/IP four-layer model.
see: Network Models, Encapsulation and Device Roles

def: Open Shortest Path First: a link-state interior routing protocol.
see: OSPFv2 Operation: Neighbors, DR/BDR, Flooding and SPF

def: The unit of data at Layer 3 (an IP packet).
see: Network Models, Encapsulation and Device Roles

def: The number of leading bits that identify the network part of an IP address (the /24 in 10.0.0.0/24).
see: IPv4 Addressing, Subnetting, VLSM and CIDR

def: An agreed set of rules and message formats for communication.
see: What Is a Network?

def: Quality of service: giving some traffic priority or guaranteed bandwidth.
see: QoS — DiffServ, Classification, Queuing, Policing and Shaping

def: Request for Comments: the numbered documents (many of them standards) that define Internet protocols.
see: Reading RFCs and IEEE Standards Efficiently

def: A device that forwards packets between networks using IP addresses and a routing table.
see: Network Models, Encapsulation and Device Roles

def: The list of networks a router knows and the next hop for each.
see: Forwarding: Routing Table, Longest-Prefix Match, Policy Routing and ECMP

def: A Layer 2 protocol that blocks redundant links so a switched network has no loops.
see: Spanning Tree: STP, RSTP and MSTP

def: A subdivision of an IP network; the mask marks which bits are the network part.
see: IPv4 Addressing, Subnetting, VLSM and CIDR

def: Transmission Control Protocol: reliable, ordered byte-stream delivery between two hosts.
see: Sockets, TCP Behavior and Linux Network Tuning

def: Time to live: a counter in each IP packet decremented by every router; the packet is dropped at 0, which stops loops.
see: IPv4 Header, Fragmentation and MTU

def: Carrying one protocol's packets inside another's (GRE, IPsec, VXLAN).
see: Tunneling Fundamentals — GRE, IP-in-IP and GRE-in-UDP

def: User Datagram Protocol: simple, unreliable, message-oriented delivery.
see: Sockets, TCP Behavior and Linux Network Tuning

def: A way to split one physical switch into several isolated Layer 2 networks.
see: VLANs, Trunking, Private VLANs and QinQ

def: A private network built across a public one, usually with tunnels and encryption.
see: IPsec and IKEv2

def: A tunnel that carries Layer 2 frames over a Layer 3 network, used in data-centre overlays.
see: VXLAN and BGP EVPN

def: Base-2 and base-16 number systems; computers store binary, people write hex as shorthand (one hex digit = 4 bits).
see: Binary, Hexadecimal and Bits

def: A bit is a 0 or 1; a byte is 8 bits (also called an octet in networking).
see: Binary, Hexadecimal and Bits

def: Small, fast memory on the processor that holds recently used data to avoid slow trips to RAM.
see: Performance-Oriented C: Caches, Branches, Data Layout and Vectorization

def: A number whose individual bits are used as on/off flags or to select bits from another number.
see: Bit Manipulation

def: How much useful data is actually delivered per second.
see: What Is a Network?
